name: Ninja
baseMeaning: A picture of a figure in black with a headband and a scarf across the face. Read in a message it lands as slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy.
tldr: 🥷 Ninja. In a chat it comes across as slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy.

contextMeanings.meaning: The plain reading: a figure in black with a headband and a scarf across the face. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Asking a friend to keep a secret 🥷

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy.
contextMeanings.example: Slipping into a plan without announcing it 🥷

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.

platformNotes.note: In Slack 🥷 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for asking a friend to keep a secret, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 🥷 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 🥷 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like slipping into a plan without announcing it. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Ninja 🥷 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like asking a friend to keep a secret is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

WhatsApp renders 🥷 exactly as the phone system does, but the keyboard keeps it in the person-fantasy section, where nobody looks unless they are hunting for it. In family threads it tends to accompany a message like slipping into a plan without announcing it.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z reaches for 🥷 to do the work of asking a friend to keep a secret, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy.

Millennials tend to send 🥷 deliberately, usually for something like slipping into a plan without announcing it, and they read slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 🥷 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 🥷 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy subtext in it.

warnings.title: 🥷 and 🕵️ get swapped
warnings.description: The Detective 🕵️ is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the detective investigates and reports back, the ninja moves without leaving a trail. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take 🥷 as something else fairly often: it gets mistaken for a cool martial-arts pose when it is really about discretion — people send it when something should stay between them. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: 🥷 Ninja Emoji - What It Actually Means in Text
seoDescription: 🥷 Ninja meaning: slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy. How the emoji is used at work, at home and in dating threads, and where it goes wrong.

longForm.overview:
The drawing of 🥷 is a figure in black with a headband and a scarf across the face. It arrived with Unicode 13.0 in the person-fantasy section, and in a conversation it does the work of a line somebody left out on purpose.

The line it stands in for is slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one — a picture carries the same meaning as the sentence it replaces, and it arrives first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets mistaken for a cool martial-arts pose when it is really about discretion — people send it when something should stay between them. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🕵️ Detective: the detective investigates and reports back, the ninja moves without leaving a trail. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

The ninja also exists in five skin tones. They are separate pages with separate copy, because picking a tone is a decision in a way that picking the plain emoji is not: it says something about who the sender thinks the reader is.

In short — the ninja reads as slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy, it is most often used for asking a friend to keep a secret or slipping into a plan without announcing it, and the five tone pages under it each say something different about who is sending it. The rest of the page takes those three apart.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
Context, not the picture, decides how this lands. 🥷 in a work thread is slipping into a plan without announcing it; 🥷 in a family thread is asking a friend to keep a secret; 🥷 in a thread with somebody you like is a way of saying something you would rather not type out.

The tone versions of the emoji make the same point from the other side. The gesture is identical in all five, and the swatch says something about the sender before a word is read.

The shortest messages are the risky ones. A lone 🥷 is the whole reply, and it is carrying a meaning nobody wrote down — slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy is the intention, but what arrives is a drawing. Everything the sentence would have disambiguated is simply missing.

Put it this way. Asking a friend to keep a secret is the job the ninja does most: it saves a sentence and lands faster than one would have. Slipping into a plan without announcing it is the job it does second: there the picture is not the point, it is the temperature of the message.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Think about what the emoji is replacing. If the sentence under it is doing the real work, 🥷 will get mistaken for a cool martial-arts pose when it is really about discretion — people send it when something should stay between them instead, and the thread ends up carrying a meaning nobody wrote.

And keep it away from first contact. There is nothing warm in the drawing, and a ninja gesture used to answer other people's messages tends to sound like it is settling a point.

Keep it out of the formal register. In a thread about somebody's work, or in a message to somebody you have not met, 🥷 reads as slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy, and formality is exactly where that reading does the most damage.

Leave 🕵️ Detective for the other message. The detective investigates and reports back, the ninja moves without leaving a trail. And keep 🥷 out of threads where somebody is hurting: it reads as slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy there, because there is nothing in the drawing that says you meant well.
longForm.howToReply:
The safe move in an unclear thread is to answer the text. 🥷 gets mistaken for a cool martial-arts pose when it is really about discretion — people send it when something should stay between them often enough that the sentence matters more than the picture.

And do not send 🥷 alone when the message underneath is supposed to be warm. A message like asking a friend to keep a secret carries the feeling; the picture on its own leaves the reader choosing between slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy and something sharper.

Start by reading what the 🥷 was doing. If it was a reaction, react: 🥷 back, and the thread is closed. If it was aimed at you, write. The difference matters, because the reply to a reaction can be a picture and the reply to a request cannot.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🥷 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under ninja show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 🥷 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🥷 is used for slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy. The drawing shows a figure in black with a headband and a scarf across the face, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🥷 and 🕵️?
faqs.answer: The detective investigates and reports back, the ninja moves without leaving a trail. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 🥷 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy, but it gets mistaken for a cool martial-arts pose when it is really about discretion — people send it when something should stay between them. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 🥷 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

conversationExamples.interpretation: A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: asking a friend to keep a secret 🥷
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: slipping into a plan without announcing it 🥷
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 🥷
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets mistaken for a cool martial-arts pose when it is really about discretion — people send it when something should stay between them more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.

conversationExamples.message: asking a friend to keep a secret 🥷
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is slipping in quietly, hiding, or asking for secrecy, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
